newsitem.title: USA: Utilities, states sue U.S. to take nuclear waste.
newsitem.headline: Utilities, states sue U.S. to take nuclear waste.

text.p: More than 30 utilities and 46 state agencies said Thursday they would seek U.S. court approval for utilities to stop payments into a federal nuclear waste fund and freeze $600 million they have already paid.

The request stemmed from a December announcement by the U.S. Energy Department that it would not be able to accept spent fuel from nuclear reactors by January 1998, as required under a 1982 law and reinforced by an appeals court decision last July.

Utilities have had to pay $600 million a year since 1983 into the federal nuclear waste fund that was meant to be used to build a permanent dump for their high-level radioactive waste beginning in 1998.
The government does not expect to have a dump ready until 2010 at the earliest, assuming that Yucca Mountain in Nevada, which is being studied, proves to be a suitable site.
The Clinton administration has refused to build an interim storage site, mainly out of concern that it would divert resources from the Yucca Mountain project.
Environmentalists argue that it would be dangerous to ship waste from utilities across the country to an interim site, then have to move it again to a permanent repository.

Michigan Attorney General Frank Kelley referred to environmentalists as "tree huggers" and said they are insisting that the utilities hold onto the waste, which was continuing to build up in pools at nuclear power plants.
"We've got caskets buried on the edge of Lake Michigan," Kelley said, adding that they were considered to be a major environmental threat.
"The purpose of this lawsuit is to prevent our customers' payments from being used to reduce the federal deficit," said Gary Johnson, general counsel of Northern States Power Co .
The coalition said that, at the same time that the government was breaking its contract with the utilities, it was accepting spent research reactor fuel from Europe.

"We find it very interesting that the DOE (Energy Department) very quickly and efficiently found space for spent fuel from foreign reactors," said Kris Sanda, Commissioner of Minnesota's Public Service Department.

The Senate last year passed a bill calling for an interim waste site to be built as soon as possible. A similar bill won overwhelming support in the House Commerce Committee but was never voted on by the full House after the Clinton administration threatened a veto.

Utilities involved in the lawsuit, to be filed on Friday, include Duke Power Co, GPU Nuclear Inc, PECO Energy Co, Consolidated Edison Co of New York Inc, Public Service Electric and Gas Co, and Baltimore Gas and Electric Co.

Energy Department officials were not immediately available to comment on the lawsuit. But Energy Secretary nominee Federico Pena said Thursday that he realized the government would be out of compliance with the law next January.
"I will make every effort to ensure we are in a position to determine the viability of Yucca Mountain as a disposal site in 1998," he said in text prepared for his confirmation hearing.
